**Who gets measles, and why?** So far, everyone in the town mixes equally. In reality, children have many more contacts than adults, mostly with other children; and where most people are vaccinated, the children who missed out are the ones still susceptible. This tutorial splits the model into age groups, each with its own immunity, mixing by a contact matrix, and reads the results by age. It then adds births and deaths, and the population and contacts of a real country.

By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

- split a model into age groups, and give a value for each group;
- give the contacts between groups as a contact matrix, and say what β means then;
- read results for one age group, or for each, and tell counts from risk;
- add births and deaths, and see why they make measles come back;
- use the age structure and contact matrix of a country.

## The model so far

This is the SEIR model from [T3 – Building a disease](t3_disease.qmd), in a town of 100,000 people, with R0 = 1.9 × 8 ≈ 15:

```{python}
import starsim as ss

S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I        # β = 1.9 per day
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)  # Latent for 10 days on average
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)   # Infectious for 8 days on average
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(I=0.001))

sim = ss.Sim(measles, total_pop=100_000, stop=ss.days(150))
sim.run()
sim.plot()
```

## Age groups, each with its own immunity

`stratify()` splits each state of a disease into groups: here by age, into 0–14, 15–64, and 65 and over, each given by its lower edge with its share of the population (30%, 60%, and 10%). The model then has a compartment for each state in each age group.

On its own, this changes nothing; age groups matter when something differs between them, such as immunity. Suppose 92% of adults under 65 and 98% of older adults are immune, but only 80% of children, since vaccine coverage has slipped. [`ss.by()`](../api/internals.parameters.qmd) gives a value for each level of a stratification, and `init` the share of each group that starts in a state; `init_n` starts 10 people infectious, as if brought in by travelers. The run is for a year, from 1 January 2025:

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ 1.9*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The share immune in each age group
    init_n = dict(I=10),                           # 10 people infectious at the start
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}) # Ages 0-14, 15-64, and 65+, with the share of people in each

settings = dict(total_pop=100_000, start='2025-01-01', stop='2026-01-01')
equal = ss.Sim(measles, label='Everyone mixes equally', **settings)
equal.run()
equal.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()
```

About 90% of the town is immune, so each case at the start infects about 1.7 others (printed as `R` at the start): a modest outbreak, peaking in early July, spread over the age groups in proportion to the susceptible people in each.

## Contacts between age groups

A **contact matrix** gives the daily contacts between age groups: row *i*, column *j* is the number of contacts one person in group *i* has with people in group *j*, as measured by contact surveys such as POLYMOD in Europe. Below, children have 10 contacts a day with other children, 6 with adults, and 1 with people 65 and over; adults and older adults have 12 each. (The numbers are illustrative, but shaped like real surveys: children mix most, mostly with each other.)

| Contacts a day, of a person aged... | ...with people 0–14 | ...with people 15–64 | ...with people 65+ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–14 | 10 | 6 | 1 |
| 15–64 | 3 | 8 | 1 |
| 65+ | 3 | 6 | 3 |

A contact between a child and an adult counts for both, so the matrix is reciprocal: the children, 30% of the town, have 6 contacts each with adults, and the adults, twice as many, 3 each with children. (Starsim notes a matrix that isn't.)

[`ss.contacts()`](../api/networks.qmd) takes the matrix, with the lower edge of each age group (`ages=`), and is given to the sim as `networks=`. With contacts, β is the daily rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, and the matrix supplies the contacts. People here average about 13.5 contacts a day, so β = 1.9 under equal mixing becomes about 0.14 per contact. (Reusing 1.9 would multiply transmission by 13.5: a β fitted under one assumption about mixing must be refitted under another.)

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
beta = ss.par(0.14, bounds=[0.05, 0.5]) # The rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day

infection   = S >> E @ beta*I       # At a rate of β times the contacts with infectious people
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
    init_n = dict(I=10),
)
measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]]) # Contacts a day, between age groups
sim = ss.Sim(measles, networks=contacts, label='Contact matrix', **settings)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()
```

## R

```r
library(starsim)

states("S E I R")
beta <- par(0.14, bounds = c(0.05, 0.5)) # The rate of infection per contact with an infectious person, per day
measles <- Disease(
  infection   = Transition(S, E, rate = beta * I), # At a rate of β times the contacts with infectious people
  progression = Transition(E, I, dur = days(10)),
  recovery    = Transition(I, R, dur = days(8)),
  init   = list(R = ss$by(age = c(0.8, 0.92, 0.98))),
  init_n = list(I = 10)
)
measles$stratify(age = list("0" = 0.3, "15" = 0.6, "65" = 0.1))

age_contacts <- contacts(ages = c(0, 15, 65), matrix = rbind(c(10, 6, 1), c(3, 8, 1), c(3, 6, 3))) # Contacts a day, between age groups
sim <- Sim(measles, networks = age_contacts, total_pop = 100000, start = "2025-01-01", stop = "2026-01-01", label = "Contact matrix")
sim$run()
sim$results$measles$infection$by("age")$plot()
```

## Explicit

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.State(name='S'), ss.State(name='E'), ss.State(name='I'), ss.State(name='R')
beta_explicit = ss.par(ss.perday(0.14), bounds=[ss.perday(0.05), ss.perday(0.5)], name='beta') # Per contact with an infectious person

measles_explicit = ss.Disease(
    transitions = [
        ss.Transition(source=S, dest=E, rate=beta_explicit*I, name='infection'),
        ss.Transition(source=E, dest=I, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(10)), name='progression'),
        ss.Transition(source=I, dest=R, dur=ss.expon(mean=ss.days(8)), name='recovery'),
    ],
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])), # The rest start in S
    init_n = dict(I=10),
    name   = 'measles',
)
measles_explicit.stratify(age=ss.levels({0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1}, kind='age')) # Age groups, which people would age through

contacts_explicit = ss.contacts(matrix=[[10, 6, 1], [3, 8, 1], [3, 6, 3]], ages=[0, 15, 65], name='contacts')
sim_explicit = ss.Sim(
    diseases  = measles_explicit,
    networks  = contacts_explicit,
    total_pop = 100_000,
    start     = '2025-01-01',
    stop      = '2026-01-01',
    dt        = ss.days(1),
    unit      = 'day',
    solver    = 'ode',
    aging     = False, # Nobody is born or dies, so nobody ages
    label     = 'Contact matrix',
)
sim_explicit.run()
sim_explicit.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()
```
:::

Starsim works out R0 from the matrix (the largest eigenvalue of the next-generation matrix), so it depends on who meets whom. R0 is about the same, 16, but the reproduction number at the start is about 2.5 rather than 1.7: the susceptible people are children, who have the most contacts, mostly with each other. To compare the two runs:

```{python}
msim = ss.parallel([equal, sim])
msim.plot('measles.infection')
```

With the contact matrix, the outbreak peaks two months sooner, twice as high, and infects about 8,800 people rather than 7,400, the extra ones all children. Assuming equal mixing would underestimate an outbreak where the gaps in immunity are in the group that mixes most.

## Results by age group

A stratified model keeps every result for each group, and totals as before (`res.infection` is all ages). [`by('age')`](../api/results.qmd) splits a result into a series per age group, and `select()` picks one group by its ages (`'0-14'`, `'15-64'`, `'65+'`):

```{python}
res = sim.results.measles
children = res.I.select(age='0-14')
print('Peak number of children infectious:', round(children.max()))
print('Infections in people 65 and over:', round(res.infection.select(age='65+').sum()))
```

`summarize()` gives each group's total over the run, the same as summing each group in turn. Counts depend on a group's size as well as its risk; dividing by its size gives the share infected (the attack rate), the risk:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
infections = res.infection.by('age').summarize()
print(infections.round())
print('Share of each group infected:')
print((infections / [30_000, 60_000, 10_000]).round(3))
```

## R

```r
res <- sim$results$measles
infections <- res$infection$by("age")$summarize()
print(round(infections))
cat("Share of each group infected:\n")
print(round(infections / c(30000, 60000, 10000), 3))
```

## Explicit

```{python}
sizes = {'0-14': 30_000, '15-64': 60_000, '65+': 10_000}
for age, size in sizes.items():
    total = res.infection.select(age=age).sum()
    print(age, ' infections:', round(total), ' share infected:', round(total/size, 3))
```
:::

Children have nearly two thirds of the infections, though under a third of the town: 18% of them are infected, over three times the share of adults.

## Births, deaths, and aging

Over decades, children are born susceptible, which is what makes measles come back: an epidemic leaves too few susceptible people for the next, until enough children are born. Births and deaths go to the sim as `demographics`: [`ss.birth()`](../api/transitions.qmd) takes a crude birth rate, here 30 a year per 1,000 people, and `ss.death()` a death rate, here 20 a year per 1,000 at every age (a simplification; [A3 – Demographics](a3_demographics.qmd) uses death rates by age). Children born into `S` move up the age groups as they age. Here is the model over 20 years, with and without them:

```{python}
demographics = [
    ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), # 30 births a year per 1,000 people
    ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)), # 20 deaths a year per 1,000 people
]
long = dict(networks=contacts, total_pop=100_000, unit='day', dt=ss.weeks(1), start='2025-01-01', stop='2045-01-01')

msim = ss.parallel({
    'No births or deaths': ss.Sim(measles, **long),
    'Births and deaths':   ss.Sim(measles, demographics=demographics, **long),
})
msim.plot('measles.I')
```

The birth and death rates are per year and the rest per day, so `unit='day'` says which unit the bare β is in ([T2 – Building a model](t2_model.qmd)). `dt=ss.weeks(1)` records results weekly; as an ODE, the model is still solved finely in between.

Without births, there is one outbreak, and then measles is gone. With births, smaller outbreaks follow a year or two apart, settling to a steady level that grows with the town: the classic pattern of measles where too few children are vaccinated (here, newborns are not vaccinated at all). In the troughs, only a handful of people are infectious, and in reality measles would often die out until brought in again. An ODE can't show this, since its expected numbers never reach zero; [T5 – Interventions and scenarios](t5_interventions.qmd) runs the model by chance instead.

## A real population

For a real place, the age groups and contacts can come from data. [`ss.population('Kenya')`](../api/people.qmd) is Kenya's population by age and sex (UN World Population Prospects), and `ss.contacts('Kenya')` a contact matrix by 5-year age group (Prem et al., 2021). `stratify()` then needs only the age groups, taking their shares from the population, and Starsim adds up the matrix into them. `total_pop` keeps the model to a town of 100,000:

```{python}
S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery,
    init   = dict(R=ss.by(age=[0.8, 0.92, 0.98])),
    init_n = dict(I=10),
)
measles.stratify(age=[0, 15, 65]) # The share in each group comes from the population

kenya = ss.Sim(measles, people=ss.population('Kenya'), networks=ss.contacts('Kenya'), **settings)
kenya.run()
kenya.results.measles.infection.by('age').plot()
```

Kenya's population is young: about 37% under 15. With the same β, R0 is about 17, since there are more contacts than in the made-up matrix, and the outbreak is larger, about 10,400 infections, nearly two thirds in children. These data are inputs, not a calibrated model: check the year, age groups, and how the survey defined contacts before relying on them. [Population data](../user_guide/populations_data.qmd) explains the data, and lists [every place there is data for](../user_guide/populations_data.qmd#appendix-every-place-and-its-data).

All of this works the same as agents (with `n_agents=`, as in [T1 – Getting started](t1_intro.qmd)): each agent has an age, and so an age group, and agents age, are born, and die. For more on stratification, such as several dimensions at once, see [T8 – Stratification and co-transmission](t8_strata.qmd) and [Stratification](../user_guide/building_stratification.qmd); for births and deaths, see [Demographics](../user_guide/populations_demographics.qmd).

## Exercises

1. Closing schools roughly halves the contacts between children. Change the matrix so that children have 5 contacts a day with other children instead of 10. How do the reproduction number at the start and the number of children infected change? Which other age groups are affected, and why?
2. Give every age group the same immunity, 90%, keeping the contact matrix. How large is the outbreak now, compared with the town above, in which the same overall share of people (about 90%) is immune? What does this say about where gaps in immunity matter most?
3. In the model with births and deaths, raise the birth rate to 45 a year per 1,000 people, as in some countries with young populations. How does the time between outbreaks change, and why?

[Solutions](solutions.qmd#t4-age-groups-and-contacts) · Next: [T5 – Interventions and scenarios](t5_interventions.qmd)

## Further reading

- [POLYMOD: Social contacts and mixing patterns relevant to the spread of infectious diseases](https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.0050074): the contact survey in eight European countries behind most age-structured models
- [Prem et al. (2021): Projecting contact matrices in 177 geographical regions](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009098): the source of `ss.contacts('Kenya')`
- [socialmixr: Social mixing matrices for infectious disease modeling](https://epiforecasts.io/socialmixr/): an R package for building contact matrices from survey data
- [epydemix: Modeling with population data](https://epydemix.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/02_Modeling_with_Population_Data.html): age-structured models with the population and contact matrices of real countries, in another Python framework
